"Pradeep, I can't do this alone anymore."
"Didi? What happened?"
"Nothing happened. That's the thing. Every day is the same. Papa's physio at seven, office at nine, Mishti's daycare at five, Papa's dinner at eight. Then Mishti wakes at two."
"You sound exhausted."
"I love him. I do. But today I was so angry I wanted to scream. And then I felt like a terrible daughter."
"You're not terrible. You're tired. I'm sorry I left it all on you."
"You're in Bengaluru, little brother."
"I can still do things. I'll handle his doctor calls and medicine orders from here. And I'll come every second weekend."
"And the day-care centre for seniors near us? I felt guilty even looking."
"Book a visit. That's not selfish, Didi. That's sensible."
Nandini breathed out. "Okay."

qa.q: Where does Pradeep live?
qa.a: He is in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when she said she wanted to scream?
qa.a: She felt angry and resentful from exhaustion, and then guilty for feeling that way about her father.

qa.q: What choices could ease Nandini's load, and why are they responsible?
qa.a: Pradeep taking the doctor calls and orders, regular weekend visits, and a seniors' day centre, because sharing care keeps Nandini able to care at all.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel hearing his sister so tired?
qa.a: He likely feels sorry and a bit guilty for leaving it all on her, and wants to take on his share.

grounding: It shows a young adult caring for an ageing parent while working and raising a child, feeling love and resentment together, and sharing tasks with a sibling and outside help.

passage:
Last winter I snapped at my mother. She had asked me to warm her water for the third time while my daughter was crying and my laptop was pinging with a client's deadline. I said, "Can't you wait one minute?" Her face fell. I went into the bathroom and cried, because I love her, and because I was so tired I could barely stand.
The next day I told Himani at work. She's been my friend since college. I expected her to say I was being ungrateful. Instead she said, "You're doing three jobs. Asking for help isn't selfish."
So I called my brother and asked him to take Sundays. We found an attendant for afternoons. I still feel a twinge of guilt some days. But I'm kinder to Amma now, and to myself.

Vinita

qa.q: What did Vinita's mother ask for the third time?
qa.a: She asked Vinita to warm her water.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling after snapping at her mother?
qa.a: Vinita felt guilty and exhausted, crying from love for Amma mixed with being so tired.

qa.q: What was the turning point that changed things for Vinita?
qa.a: Telling Himani and hearing that asking for help isn't selfish, which led to calling the brother and finding an afternoon attendant.

qa.q: How did Vinita's mother react to being snapped at?
qa.a: Her face fell, showing she was hurt by the sharp words.

grounding: It shows a young adult caring for an ageing parent while working and raising a child, feeling love, duty and resentment, and choosing shared and outside help.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Friday
Aditi has been with us three years and is one of our best. Over the last two months she has arrived late, left early, and today I found her crying in the pantry. She told me her father has had a stroke and moved in with her, her toddler is teething, and she is doing everything herself while working full time. She said, 'I love my father. But some days I resent all of it, and then I hate myself.' I told her those feelings make sense together. We agreed she can shift her hours to ten to six for now. I also suggested she ask her brothers for regular help and look at a day-care centre for her father. She worried that was selfish. I said it was responsible. She has promised to call her brothers this weekend.
Mridul

qa.q: Where did Mridul find Aditi crying?
qa.a: In the pantry.

qa.q: What is Aditi feeling about caring for her father?
qa.a: She feels love and duty but also resentment, and then guilt for resenting it.

qa.q: What did Mridul suggest that could help?
qa.a: Shifting her hours, asking her brothers for regular help and looking at a day-care centre for her father.

qa.q: How might Aditi's brothers be affected by her call?
qa.a: They may feel surprised or guilty, but it gives them a chance to share the care.

grounding: Shows a young adult caring for a parent while working and raising a child, feeling love, duty and resentment, and a supervisor framing shared and outside help as responsible.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 pm
Mummyji called for help four times tonight. The baby woke twice. I have a client presentation at nine tomorrow. Since her stroke in March, she's lived with us, and I do her physio, her meals and her medicines, plus the baby, plus the job. I love her. She's been kind to me since the day I married into this family. And tonight I stood in the kitchen and thought, I can't do this, I don't want to do this, and then I felt disgusting for thinking it. I'm writing it so I stop pretending. Tomorrow I'm going to ask Uday, my brother-in-law, to take Mummyji every weekend. And I'm booking the day-care nurse three mornings a week. That isn't abandoning her. It's how I keep going.
Shreya

qa.q: How many times did Mummyji call for help tonight?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What did Shreya feel standing in the kitchen?
qa.a: Shreya felt exhausted and resentful, then disgusted at the thought.

qa.q: What steps is Shreya planning?
qa.a: Asking Uday to take Mummyji every weekend and booking a day-care nurse three mornings a week.

qa.q: How might Uday respond to Shreya's request?
qa.a: Uday may be surprised at how much Shreya has carried, and hopefully willing to share the weekends.

grounding: Shows a young adult caring for an ageing parent-in-law while working and raising a baby, feeling love and resentment, and choosing shared and outside help.

passage: Neelam's day in Sultanpur started at five: her mother Ganga's tablets set out, Chhotu's milk, Amma's breakfast, then the walk to the anganwadi where she worked till two. Evenings were Amma's bath, Chhotu's fever, Amma calling from the cot every half hour. One night, spooning rice into Amma's mouth, Neelam caught herself thinking, "When do I get to be tired?" Then she felt ashamed. Amma had carried her on her hip through two floods. On Sunday Neelam phoned her brother in Lucknow. "I can't do all of it. Arrange a day nurse for two afternoons a week, and come the first weekend of every month." He was quiet, then agreed. The next month Neelam slept till seven on a Sunday for the first time in a year.

qa.q: Where does Neelam work until two?
qa.a: At the anganwadi.

qa.q: What did Neelam feel after thinking "When do I get to be tired?"
qa.a: She felt ashamed of the resentment, remembering how Ganga had carried her through two floods.

qa.q: Why is asking her brother responsible rather than selfish?
qa.a: Sharing the care and bringing in a day nurse keeps Neelam able to look after both Ganga and Chhotu well, instead of burning out.

qa.q: How might Ganga be affected by Neelam's exhaustion?
qa.a: Ganga may sense it in the hurried days, and could feel more settled with steadier, shared care.

grounding: Shows a young adult caring for an ageing parent while working and raising a child, feeling love, duty and resentment, and sharing tasks with a sibling and outside help.
